title: Michi and the Blue Truck
summary: Out of curiosity, Michi climbs into a blue truck and ends up on the other side of the city, far away from the home where someone is always waiting for him.

scenes.text:
Michi was a tabby cat, with stripes the colour of milky coffee.

He lived with Elena in a little house on Almond Tree Street, next to a bakery that smelled of warm bread all morning.

Every afternoon, Elena came home from school, picked him up and asked:

"Did you wait for me all day?"

And Michi purred with his eyes shut. That was his favourite place in the world.

But that Thursday, a blue truck stopped outside the bakery.

It had boxes in the back, and it smelled of new things, of faraway places. Michi felt a tickle at the tip of his tail: the tickle of curiosity.

He looked at the truck. He looked at the boxes. And without thinking too hard about it, he jumped.

Between the boxes it smelled of cardboard and wood. Michi found a soft little corner, turned round three times and curled up like a bread roll.

Then the engine coughed, and the truck set off.

At first it was fun. The truck rocked like a cradle, and the air tickled his whiskers.

Michi yawned. He closed one eye. He closed the other.

And he fell asleep.

When he woke up, the truck had stopped. Michi poked his nose out and hopped down to the ground.

There was no bakery. There were no almond trees. His house wasn't there.

There were enormous buildings, blinking traffic lights and people hurrying along without looking down.

Michi sat with his tail pressed tight against his body. He was far away. Very, very far away.

The city made an enormous noise. Horns, brakes, a siren in the distance.

Michi walked close to the walls, trying to make himself small.

Suddenly, behind a fence, a huge dog appeared, and barked.

Michi sprang so high that he nearly touched a sign. And he dashed under a car, with his heart going thump-thump-thump in his ears.

"I want to go home," he said quietly. "I want my blanket. I want Elena."

He waited for a long time. The dog got bored, and the street grew calmer.

Michi poked out one whisker. Then half his nose. Then a paw.

And he decided he wasn't going to stay crying under a car.

On top of a lamp post sat a plump grey pigeon. She had been watching him for a while.

"You're lost, aren't you?" she said, coming down to the pavement in a flutter. "I can tell from your ears."

"I live next to a bakery," said Michi. "It smells of warm bread. There are almond trees in the street."

"I know that neighbourhood. I fly all over the city."

The pigeon leaned her beak close, as if she were telling him a secret.

"Always walk towards where the sun goes down. Cross the big park. Then the market. At the end you'll see a bridge over the river: cross it without being scared, and you'll be nearly there."

"And what if I get lost again?"

"Close your eyes," said the pigeon, "and sniff."

Michi looked at the sun, which was already starting to sink.

"Thank you, pigeon. I'm going to get there."

The big park appeared round a corner, green and enormous, as if someone had tucked a piece of countryside inside the city.

Michi went in under a bench. The grass was cool, and the noise of the cars stayed outside.

He could hear birds, a ball, a swing.

Two children wanted to stroke him, and Michi let them for a moment, because their hands were like Elena's. But when the smaller one tried to hug him, Michi slipped gently away.

He couldn't stay. Someone was waiting for him.

On the far side of the park, the sun was already hiding among the trees. Michi walked faster.

The market was a tunnel of smells. Oranges, coriander, fish, wet flowers.

Michi wove between baskets and table legs, dodging hurrying shoes. Somebody was sweeping. Somebody was pulling down a metal shutter.

From on top of some boxes, a very thin orange cat looked at him and miaowed.

"And who are you?"

"I'm on my way home," said Michi.

"Good luck, then," said the other cat, and moved aside.

At that moment, Michi smelled something wonderful: fish. The lady at the last stall, the one in the blue apron, bent down and left him a little piece on some paper.

"Eat up, little one," she said. "You're a long way from home, aren't you?"

Michi ate every bit and licked his whiskers. For the first time all day, his tummy was happy. And night was beginning to fall.

The bridge appeared at the end of a long street, with two rows of lamps lit up.

Below, the river flowed slowly, talking to itself.

Michi stopped at the start. The bridge was very long, and he was very small.

"No being scared," he told himself, just as the pigeon had said. "One paw, then another paw."

And he began to cross.

The breeze from the river combed his fur the wrong way. Halfway across he stopped to look at the city lights reflected in the water, trembling like golden fish.

It was beautiful. Michi twitched his ears and carried on to the other side.

On the other side of the river, the streets were narrower and quieter.

Suddenly, Michi stopped with one paw in the air.

He closed his eyes, the way the pigeon had taught him. And he sniffed.

Bread.

Warm bread. That bread.

It was a very thin thread of smell coming from the corner. Michi followed it with his nose in the air, and three streets later he saw something he knew: a crooked tree, a green gate, a puddle where he always drank.

The almond trees! His street!

Then he ran.

He had never run like that, with his ears flat back and his tail up like a flag. He passed the closed bakery, he passed the usual lamp post, and he skidded to a stop in front of his house.

Michi scratched at the wood and called out with all his might.

Inside came the sound of running feet, a chair scraping, and Elena's voice:

"Mum! It's him! It's him!"

And all at once, open flew the door.

There was Elena, in her pyjamas, her hair a mess, her eyes enormous. She picked him up and squeezed him so tight that Michi had to wriggle to get comfortable.

She told him everything at once: that she had put up posters on the lamp posts, that she had left a bowl in the window every night, that she hadn't wanted pudding even once.

Michi purred so loudly that his whole body shook.

"He's thin and very dirty," said Elena's mum, checking his paws. "But he's all in one piece."

Then came the shortest bath in history, a towel that smelled clean and a gentle brush.

Elena carried him to her room and put him in his usual spot: at the foot of the bed, on the checked blanket.

"Tomorrow you can tell me what you did," she whispered. "Now it's time for sleep."

Michi kneaded the blanket with his paws, turned round three times and curled up into a ball.

There were no more trucks, or dogs, or bridges. Just Elena's hand on his back, going slowly up and down.

And from deep in the chest of a happy cat, there came a little snore.
